item.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
item.description:
Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics

Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. However, changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence.

🧩 How it works

  • Integrates an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning.
  • Features a harness for planning and tool orchestration.
  • Utilizes a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution.
  • Assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis.
  • Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage.
  • Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing.
  • Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification.

💡 Why it matters

  • The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency.
  • Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points.
  • In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

#SportsAnalytics #AIAgents #MachineLearning #ConversationalAI

Source: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality? Source: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics

item.title: NVIDIA Releases cuDSS 1.0 and DuckDB Sirius Extension
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases cuDSS 1.0 and DuckDB Sirius Extension

NVIDIA has released version 1.0 of its cuDSS library for sparse linear systems and collaborated with DuckLabs to release Sirius, a GPU-accelerated extension for DuckDB, enabling high-performance analytical queries on NVIDIA hardware.

🧩 How cuDSS Works

The cuDSS library is designed to solve large sparse linear systems for engineering and scientific simulations. It targets numerically challenging sparse systems, particularly symmetric indefinite ones, by offering symmetry-preserving matching and scaling as well as Bunch-Kaufman pivoting.

  • Matching and Scaling: Uses the HSL MC64 algorithm from the HSL collection of Fortran codes. This feature preserves symmetry and is enabled by default in cuDSS 1.0, improving accuracy and reducing memory and performance penalties associated with previous nonsymmetric matching.
  • Bunch-Kaufman Pivoting: Allows 2×2 pivots to maintain factorization stability while preserving symmetry. The algorithm applies a local test to each column to choose between 1×1 pivots, interchanged 1×1 pivots, or 2×2 blocks.
  • Default Configuration: cuDSS 1.0 defaults to using matching and scaling with CUDSS_MATCHING_ALG_MAX_DIAG_PRODUCT and Bunch-Kaufman pivoting with CUDSS_PIVOT_BUNCH_KAUFMAN. Users can restore previous behavior using CUDSS_CONFIG_FORCE_NONSYMMETRIC_MATCHING.

📊 cuDSS Performance

Benchmark matrices for cuDSS were selected from semiconductor design, manufacturing, and computer-aided engineering workflows, including circuit simulation, TCAD, thermal, structural, electromagnetic, and fluid dynamics. Performance was benchmarked against Intel MKL version 2026.1.0 using an NVIDIA B200 GPU and an Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPU.

Phase Geometric-Mean Speedup
Analysis 2.5x
Numerical Factorization 5.9x
Triangular Solve 151x

cuDSS performance has improved over previous releases, with optimizations for superpanels in factorization, multithreaded analysis, and tuned solve-phase kernels. Developers can access these gains by upgrading without changing application code.

🐝 Sirius for DuckDB

Sirius is an open-source, GPU-native SQL engine developed through a collaboration between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and NVIDIA, released as a DuckDB core extension in partnership with DuckLabs.

  • Integration: Developers can install and load Sirius using two SQL commands (INSTALL sirius; and LOAD sirius;). It requires DuckDB 2.0 and an NVIDIA GPU with a compatible driver.
  • Architecture: DuckDB handles SQL parsing and optimization, while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU using a CUDA backend.
  • Performance: In TPC-H benchmarks with data stored in Amazon S3, Sirius delivered significant speedups over CPU-based DuckDB.
    • At Scale Factor 1,000 (1 TB), total query runtime fell from 347.3 seconds to 63.2 seconds.
    • At Scale Factor 3,000 (3 TB), runtime dropped from 752.4 seconds to 160.6 seconds, a 4.69x speedup.
    • With tuned settings, a two-GPU AWS instance configuration achieved 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best CPU-based configurations, reducing query-time compute cost by up to approximately 79%.

🚀 Availability

The general availability of cuDSS marks it as a production-ready library for commercial applications. Sirius is available as a DuckDB core extension, with a download size of approximately 700 MB.

#NVIDIA #cuDSS #DuckDB #GPU #HighPerformanceComputing

Source: Accelerating Direct Sparse Solvers for Computational Engineering with NVIDIA cuDSS 1.0 | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: AWS Quick adds Meta ads AI connector for marketing workflows
item.description:
AWS Quick adds Meta ads AI connector for marketing workflows

AWS Quick has added a Meta ads AI connector, enabling marketers to create, manage, and analyze campaigns using natural language while staying connected to the Meta ad management network.

🔍 Overview

The connector addresses the friction of manual data handling in marketing teams. Previously, data such as campaign results, creative assets, and inventory lived in separate systems like Meta Ads Manager, shared storage, and data lakes. Analysts often had to export reports and manually update campaigns, leading to slow insights. With the new connector, marketing teams can use one place to go from campaign planning to execution, acting on business insights directly in their ads without tool switching.

🧩 How it works

The Meta ads AI connector gives AWS Quick access to ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server operations. Installation involves navigating to Customize > Connectors in AWS Quick, signing in with Facebook, and selecting which Pages, Businesses, and Instagram accounts AWS Quick can access. Once connected, users can interact with the system via natural language prompts. The system can combine Meta ad management data with first- and third-party data sources to generate dashboards, documents, slide decks, and automated workflows. It also integrates with fal.ai’s image, audio, and video models within the same workflow to test creative ideas.

⚙️ Key details

The connector supports specific capabilities for managing ad lifecycle tasks:

  • Plan and launch campaigns: Drafts campaign, ad set, and ad settings from an approved brief; flags missing budget and audience decisions; runs pre-launch checks for naming, UTM tags, budget, and special ad categories.
  • Analyze and share performance: Tracks spend, CTR, and ROAS at various levels; compares results to the media plan; builds weekly decks of top ads, weak ads, and next tests; allows leaders to review decks and ask follow-up questions.
  • Refresh creative and audiences: Flags creative fatigue when frequency rises and CTR falls.
  • Pulling insights and creation: Supports creating product catalogs and editing or creating new campaigns.

The system also executes specific prompt-based outputs, such as turning past campaign results into an eight-slide launch-plan deck or building a dashboard comparing spend, leads, and cost per lead for two ad sets.

💡 Why it matters

By automating the path from insight to action, the connector reduces manual handoffs and tool switching. Marketing teams can spend more time reaching customers and testing more creative ideas, as supported by the integration of fal.ai media models.

#AWS #MetaAds #MarketingAutomation #AI

Source: Meta ads is now available in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS WAF Introduces New Security Analytics Dashboard
item.description:
AWS WAF Introduces New Security Analytics Dashboard

AWS has introduced a new security analytics dashboard for AWS WAF, providing a single global page to investigate traffic across all protection packs (web ACLs), Regional resources, and Amazon CloudFront distributions. This update builds on the 2024 traffic overview dashboard by offering a consolidated view that helps users act on findings faster.

🔍 Overview

The new dashboard is designed to help users investigate and contain threats faster while reducing false positives that block real customers. Key aspects of the update include:

  • A single global page for investigating traffic across all protection packs (web ACLs).
  • Coverage of Regional resources and Amazon CloudFront distributions.
  • No need to build or maintain a custom log analytics pipeline.
  • Built on full-fidelity request data rather than samples.
  • Two primary use cases demonstrated: investigating a traffic spike and tuning rules to reduce false positives.

🧩 How It Works

To access the dashboard, users navigate to the AWS WAF console and select “Security analytics” in the navigation pane. The interface allows users to narrow the view to specific protection packs and set time ranges.

  • Global View: The dashboard displays request data across all protection packs in the account. Selecting “All protection packs” shows a comprehensive view.
  • Traffic Breakdown: The top of the page shows total requests split by action: Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, and Challenge.
  • Charts and Widgets: The “Requests chart” visualizes traffic changes over time, while widgets below display top values for specific dimensions. Users can split the Requests chart by dimensions such as Host, Rule triggered, Country, or JA4.
  • Host Grouping: Grouping or filtering by Host identifies which domains are under attack or experiencing spikes, even when a single protection pack protects multiple domains or a domain spans several protection packs.
  • Labels and Detections: AWS Managed Rules add labels (e.g., Bot Control categories, verification status, and signals like non_browser_user_agent). Users can also create custom labels. Because labels are recorded even when a rule is set to count-only, filtering by a label shows what a rule detected across all protection packs without changing how traffic is handled.
  • Filters and Actions: Filters apply to the entire dashboard, updating the action split, Requests chart, widgets, and request list. Users can select any value in a widget to focus on it, remove it, or block it.
  • Request Details: For individual requests, the dashboard displays HTTP fields such as host, path, headers, user agent, and JA4 fingerprint. It also shows which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted.

⚙️ Key Details

Previously, accessing this level of detail required working from a limited sample of requests or setting up and querying custom AWS WAF logs. The new dashboard makes this data available directly. Additionally, the current dashboard view is saved in the user’s browser.

💡 Why It Matters

This tool allows security teams to move from reactive log analysis to proactive investigation and containment. By providing full-fidelity data without the overhead of maintaining custom pipelines, organizations can more effectively tune their rules to minimize false positives and protect their infrastructure.

#AWS #WAF #WebSecurity #CloudSecurity #DataAnalytics

Source: Introducing the new AWS WAF security analytics dashboard | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Quick User Group DC Meetup Highlights FIG Analytics Platform
item.description:
AWS Quick User Group DC Meetup Highlights FIG Analytics Platform

On Wednesday, October 7, 2026, data leaders, developers, and practitioners gathered at the AWS Skills Center in Arlington, Virginia, for the AWS Quick User Group DC meetup. The session brought together founders, software engineers, and enterprise leaders, including a team from Financial Independence Group (FIG), to explore AWS Quick and participate in a hands-on application-building exercise.

🔍 Overview

  • Event: AWS Quick User Group DC meetup
  • Date: October 7, 2026
  • Location: AWS Skills Center, Arlington, Virginia
  • Attendees: Data leaders, developers, practitioners, founders, software engineers, enterprise leaders, and FIG team
  • Speaker: Vanessa Gonzalez, Vice President of AI at Financial Independence Group (FIG)

🧩 How it works

AWS Quick capabilities demonstrated at the meetup:

  • Agents and skills: Turn natural-language questions into multi-step reusable actions that aid in decision making across enterprise data
  • Built-in integrations: Connect tools like Salesforce, Slack, Google Drive, and Microsoft 365, breaking down data silos
  • Unified workspace: A cohesive environment that bridges research, automated visual generation, and business artifact creation (presentations, documents, and spreadsheets) directly where users work

⚙️ Key details

FIG’s implementation of AWS Quick:

  • Role: AWS Quick serves as FIG’s “single front door” for enterprise analytics
  • Data scope: Brings together structured data (CRM systems, databases, finance data) and unstructured content (internal knowledge bases, policy documents, collateral) through a governed data layer
  • AI analytics loop: Moves from reporting on what already happened to a continuous cycle: Ask → Analyze → Automate → Act
  • Centralized discovery: Analytics portal organized by business area (sales, operations, marketing, commissions) with built-in AI chat assistants so teams can talk directly to their documents and datasets
  • Democratized insights: Self-service exploration tools for non-technical business users, plus a learning hub that builds prompt engineering and AI skills across teams while keeping proper governance in place

🚀 Availability

Hands-on results from the meetup:

  • Every attendee successfully designed and launched a custom application in AWS Quick within 50 minutes
  • A subset of six participants built multi-step, event-triggered flows that handle repetitive data tasks
  • These flows replace manual reporting handoffs with automated, repeatable pipelines
  • New ideas now take hours or even minutes to build, not weeks or months

💡 Why it matters

  • FIG moved from existing analytics to AWS Quick to bring AI into its dashboards, reporting, and analytics
  • The platform enables a governed transition from static reporting to an continuous AI-driven analytics loop
  • Self-service tooling with embedded learning reduces time-to-insight for non-technical users while maintaining governance
  • Rapid application development (50 minutes for a custom app) accelerates organizational experimentation and deployment

#AWS #AIAnalytics #EnterpriseData #DataGovernance #WorkflowAutomation #BusinessIntelligence

Source: From reporting to reasoning: Getting enterprise data ready for AI agents | Amazon Web Services

item.title: BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK for AI Agent Observability
item.description:
BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK for AI Agent Observability

An open-source Python SDK for analyzing, evaluating, and curating agent traces stored in BigQuery has been released. Built on top of the BigQuery Agent Analytics, it provides a consumption-layer toolkit for agent observability, analysis, evaluation, and advanced capabilities like the Agent Context Graph — extracting decision traces from your agent’s context graph — at scale.

🔍 Overview

  • An open-source Python SDK for analyzing, evaluating, and curating agent traces stored in BigQuery.
  • Built on top of the BigQuery Agent Analytics, it provides a consumption-layer toolkit for agent observability, analysis, evaluation, and advanced capabilities like the Agent Context Graph — extracting decision traces from your agent’s context graph — at scale.

⚙️ Key details

  • The BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK connects your AI agent telemetry in BigQuery to a rich set of evaluation, observability, and analytics capabilities.
  • It is designed for ML engineers, data scientists, and platform teams who run agents in production and need to understand agent behavior, measure quality, and detect regressions — all through BigQuery SQL or Python.
  • Features include:
    • Trace reconstruction and DAG visualization
    • Per-event-type BigQuery views
    • Observability dashboards (Looker Studio, Streamlit, SQL, and BigFrames), including BQCA Prompt & Response Logging dashboards for Conversational Analytics data agents
    • System metrics (latency, turn count, tool call error rate, token efficiency, time to first token, cost)
    • Performance Metrics (correctness, hallucination, sentiment, efficiency, etc)
    • Multi-trial system and performance metrics
    • Grader composition (weighted, binary, majority strategies)
    • Eval suite lifecycle management with graduation and saturation detection
    • Static quality validation (ambiguous tasks, class imbalance, suspicious thresholds)
    • BigQuery AI.GENERATE, AI.EMBED, AI.CLASSIFY
    • Anomaly detection and latency forecasting
    • Categorical (Hatteras-style) evaluation via BigFrames
    • Agent Context Graph — extract decision traces from your agent’s context graph: the requests an agent handled, the options it weighed, and the outcomes it committed, materialized into a queryable BigQuery property graph (GQL traversal, scheduled refresh via bqaa context-graph)
    • Long-horizon cross-session memory
    • Multi-stage agent insights pipeline
    • Drift detection for golden vs production question distributions
    • 12+ commands for diagnostics, evaluation, and CI/CD integration
    • Remote Function (BigQuery SQL via Cloud Run)
    • Python UDF scoring kernels
    • Streaming evaluation (Cloud Scheduler + Cloud Run)
    • Continuous query templates

🚀 Availability

  • Python 3.10+
  • A Google Cloud project with BigQuery enabled
  • Agent traces already written to BigQuery by one of the producers above

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a comprehensive toolkit for AI agent observability, analysis, evaluation, and advanced capabilities at scale.
  • Designed for ML engineers, data scientists, and platform teams to understand agent behavior, measure quality, and detect regressions.
  • Enables trace reconstruction, DAG visualization, and observability dashboards for better agent performance insights.
  • Facilitates system metrics, performance metrics, and eval suite lifecycle management for continuous improvement.
  • Supports anomaly detection, latency forecasting, and categorical evaluation for robust agent performance.
  • Provides the Agent Context Graph for extracting decision traces and long-horizon cross-session memory for enhanced agent capabilities.
  • Offers multi-stage agent insights pipeline and drift detection for golden vs production question distributions.
  • Includes 12+ commands for diagnostics, evaluation, and CI/CD integration for seamless workflow integration.
  • Supports Remote Function, Python UDF scoring kernels, and streaming evaluation for flexible evaluation capabilities.
  • Provides continuous query templates for efficient query management.

#BigQuery #AIAgents #AgentAnalytics #MLOps #DataScience

Source: GoogleCloudPlatform/BigQuery-Agent-Analytics-SDK

item.title: Databricks introduces Skills for Genie One
item.description:
Databricks introduces Skills for Genie One

Databricks has introduced a new feature for Genie One called Skills, which adds a layer of control by defining specific workflow recipes that the agent can follow on demand to ensure consistent formats and outputs.

🧩 How it works

A skill is a durable, reusable asset that serves as a written record of how a team works, using plain language and the open Agent Skills format. Genie One leverages skills either when called directly by the user or when it decides a skill is relevant to the request.

  • Scope and Isolation: Guidance stays with the specific task rather than spilling into other work. Because Genie One only reads the skills it needs, keeping them specific and focused is advantageous for testing, fixing, and reusing them.
  • Chainable Assets: Small skills can be chained together; for example, updating a style guidelines skill once allows every other skill that uses it to pick up the change.
  • Judgment vs. Routines: While dashboards do the same thing every time, skills allow Genie One to make decisions, such as choosing the most important changes for leadership or following unusual results until they make sense.
  • Strict Rules: Skills define what must always appear, what to do when something is missing, and thresholds that decide what gets a closer look. For instance, a trading brief might always include a watch list even if nothing breached a threshold.

⚙️ Key details

Skills distinguish themselves from Genie Agents and Genie Ontology by focusing on the method rather than domain knowledge:

Component Function
Genie Ontology Tells Genie One what things mean.
Genie Agent Domain expert for one area (e.g., sales, finance, HR); knows metric definitions, tables, joins, and business rules.
Skill Recipe for a specific task: the steps, checklist, and output format.

For example, a sales pipeline Genie Agent knows the pipeline tables and stage definitions, while a “weekly forecast risk memo” skill instructs Genie One to compare current and previous pipeline data, flag slipped deals, and produce a one-page memo. The Genie Agent supplies domain knowledge, and the skill supplies the workflow.

💡 Why it matters

You can build a skill directly in Genie One by explaining your workflow in detail once, prompting the agent to interview you before writing the skill. Genie One draws on existing knowledge through Genie Ontology to focus questions on how you work rather than what your data means. Answering in plain language is enough for Genie One to write the skill. Once built, a skill can be published through Unity Gateway and used by any agent that supports MCP, including coding agents teams already use.

Consider using a skill when you find yourself explaining the same thing to Genie One more than once.

#Databricks #GenieOne #AISkills #MCP #WorkflowAutomation

Source: Teach Genie One your workflows: The ultimate guide for skills in Genie One

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base adds tabular search for agentic retrieval
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base adds tabular search for agentic retrieval

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base adds tabular search, enabling agentic retrieval to answer analytical questions from tables combined with related documents.

🔍 Overview

  • Tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base lets agents get answers from tables through agentic retrieval.
  • When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets.
  • It combines results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps.
  • Example: A finance team closing the quarter asks “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer; it depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook.
  • Most teams keep narratives and data in the same place; for example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon S3 bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs.

🔧 How It Works

  • Tabular search is part of the agentic retrieval flow; there’s nothing to turn on.
  • When a question needs the data in a table, the request moves through these stages:
    • Retrieve: Passages come back, including passages from a table file.
    • Plan: The agent uses the question and table structure to determine whether to run code over one or more retrieved tables.
    • Stage: Tabular search copies the original file into an isolated sandbox with no network access.
    • Compute: Model-written code runs over the whole table or sheet.
    • Return: The agent gets back only what the code prints, such as totals or matching rows.
    • Answer: The agent answers from the results and the passages, with citations.
  • Tabular search starts when retrieved passages come from a CSV, XLSX, or XLS file and the question needs a calculation across rows or a lookup of specific values.
  • The Retrieve API keeps returning passages and doesn’t run code.
  • Tables lose information when split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape:
    • Long tables: A table with thousands of rows spans many passages, and retrieval returns only the few that best match the question. An answer built from them uses a handful of rows, so a total, a comparison, or a threshold check can be incomplete.
    • Wide tables: In a table with hundreds of columns, one row can hold more text than a passage or a search model takes in at once. As a result, values in later columns are harder to match.
    • Long passages from wide tables can also match many unrelated questions and push more relevant passages out of the results.
  • Retrieval also has to match a question to the right table; questions use business terms such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers.
  • A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search.
  • The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy.
  • Tabular search therefore splits the work: retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table.
  • Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Tabular search is built for questions that need calculations or lookups over the table files it retrieves.
  • Running code adds at least one more agent turn, so answers that use table data take longer than text-only answers.
  • Governed metrics, recurring dashboards, warehouse-scale joins, and reporting controls still belong in business intelligence (BI) tools.
  • Tabular search works on table files stored next to your documents, and you don’t define a schema.
  • In this solution, an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base stores your CSV and Excel files together with related documents.
  • Then an agent running Amazon Bedrock’s Claude 3 reads the files and decides whether to run code over them to answer specific questions.
  • The trace shows which files the code was run over.
  • To see what tabular search can do, build a knowledge base from a set of sample finance files, then run a question that needs a calculation across rows and check the trace to see which file the code read.
  • The knowledge base automatically converts the XLSX workbook to a CSV format for analysis.
  • The example question “Which departments must write variance commentary?” needs data from three sources: the variance threshold from the policy, the list of departments and their variances from the workbook, and the list of revised budgets from the memo.
  • Sending an AgenticRetrieveStream request with that prompt returns the full answer and citations to the sources.
  • The trace shows which passages the search model found and which of those passages the agent used to build the answer; for tabular search, it also shows which file the code was run over.
  • In the trace, look for a passage that says: “Based on the provided variance data, the following departments exceed the 5% threshold and require variance commentary: Sales (6.3%), Engineering (6.1%), and Operations (5.5%).”
  • The source for that passage isn’t the P&L workbook; it’s a file that begins with “thought” and ends with “.csv”.
  • To see what that file contains, copy the “sourceUri” value, including the “s3://” prefix, into the URL bar of a browser logged into AWS, such as the AWS Management Console.
  • When you open the URL, you see the result of the calculation over the P&L workbook.
  • The file contains the question, the revised budgets from the memo, and the calculated variances.
  • Looking back at the trace, the agent used only two passages from the original files: the list of revised budgets from the memo and the definition of the variance threshold from the policy.
  • It didn’t refer to the workbook at all because it used the computed results instead.

💡 Why It Matters

  • With retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can customize answers per tenant.
  • The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer.
  • You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request.
  • Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next.
  • For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application.
  • Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it.
  • When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the new version when you’re ready.
  • AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions, serves as an example; its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants built on the same documents; AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant, and each needs a different answer; a customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note; to keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base, however agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them.
  • Retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary; use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve.
  • Tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote.
  • A retrieval instruction has four fields for these differences: persona, who the assistant is including identity, tone, and language; answerFormat, how the answer is structured including how it cites sources; retrievalGuidance, how the agent interprets the question and what it prioritizes when it searches; answerPolicy, whether and how to answer, including questions outside scope.
  • The persona, answerFormat, and answerPolicy fields apply only when generateResponse is true, which is the default, and retrievalGuidance applies either way.
  • An instruction belongs to your AWS account and AWS Region, not to a knowledge base, and goes through these stages: Create (CreateRetrievalInstruction returns HTTP 202), Review (Amazon Bedrock reviews the instruction’s fields asynchronously, and you poll for the result), Activate (a passing review makes the instruction ACTIVE, and DRAFT points to its current content), Version (CreateRetrievalInstructionVersion saves an immutable numbered version), Apply (a request names the instruction and, optionally, a version, which defaults to DRAFT), Report (the first Planning trace event includes appliedInstruction).
  • Instructions set voice, format, conventions, and policy wording; they don’t limit which documents the agent can retrieve, and they don’t choose the tenant’s own values, which come from naming the tenant in the request; use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to limit what each tenant can retrieve, and each tenant gets its own instruction and metadata filter; your backend chooses both from the authenticated tenant, so one shared knowledge base can serve every tenant; a request can query a shared global knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base together, each with its own filter.

#AmazonBedrock #TabularSearch #AgenticRetrieval

Source: Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services Source: Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Analytics agents boost actionable insights to 48% but half remain ineffective
item.description:
Analytics agents boost actionable insights to 48% but half remain ineffective

Generative AI has broadened enterprise analytics, and the next wave—agentic AI—aims to automate whole workflows and act on the insights they generate.

🔍 Overview

  • Analytics agents are software assistants that surface descriptive and prescriptive insights for business users.
  • While most respondents praise the quality of descriptive insights, reviews of prescriptive insights are mixed.
  • Failure to produce business‑improving insights harms ROI, and flawed insights can cause reputational or financial damage.

📈 Performance Update

  • 48% of insights generated by analytics agents now lead to actions that improve the business. This is up from 37% a year ago.
  • More than half of the insights still do not help the business.
  • A small cohort called insight leaders achieves >70% actionable‑improvement rate and rates the quality of their agents’ insights higher than the overall respondents, especially for prescriptive insights.

⚠️ Challenges

  • The top reason agents produce substandard insights is a lack of business context (cited by 55% of executives).
  • Fragmented or inaccessible data is the second major factor (45%).
  • 52% of surveyed organizations say agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and acted upon.
  • Only 24% can evaluate all agent insights; most evaluations are done case‑by‑case and are human‑intensive.

🛠️ Improvement Initiatives

  • AI and data governance initiatives are a priority for 60% of companies to improve insight quality.
  • Adding a semantic layer to the data architecture is being pursued by 45% of respondents; experts interviewed stress that a semantic layer is crucial for high‑performing agents.
  • Insight leaders report fewer struggles with accessing business context.

🚀 Outlook

  • Agentic AI promises to move beyond delivering insights to automating entire workflows and taking actions based on those insights.
  • Closing the gap in context and data accessibility, and managing insight volume, are critical steps for more organizations to join the insight‑leader group.

#AIAnalytics #AgenticAI #EnterpriseAI #DataGovernance

Source: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics

item.title: Amazon Quick UK User Group Shares 2026 Yearly Roundup Following Three Meetups
item.description:
Amazon Quick UK User Group Shares 2026 Yearly Roundup Following Three Meetups

The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom has released its 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting the progress and momentum across all three quarterly meetups held since the community’s launch.

🔍 Overview

The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences. All three events took place at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London, drawing over 150 attendees with focus centered on agentic AI and Amazon Quick.

⚙️ Key details

The group’s quarterly gatherings evolved across each session:

  • Q1: Focused on introductions and product demonstrations for the community’s inaugural gathering.
  • Q2: Included an icebreaker quiz alongside a focused hands-on workshop covering Amazon Quick Flows and automation.
  • Q3: Featured a specialist panel, a group quiz, and a dedicated networking session at the end.

At each meetup, participants engaged in a 75-minute hands-on workshop starting around 9:45 AM, working inside provisioned sandbox accounts to test tools and features.

🛠️ Tools and capabilities

Attendees participated in hands-on workshop sessions testing several tools and features:

  • Amazon Quick Chat Agents: Created custom chat agents without writing code to connect to tools, access data, and take actions on behalf of users.
  • Amazon Quick Desktop: Ran directly on attendees’ laptops, connecting to local files and using a connector to access Outlook.
  • Amazon Quick Apps: Converted plain-language descriptions into functional web applications.
  • Amazon Quick Flows & Automate: Automated processes across workflows.
  • Amazon Quick Research: Reduced the time required to complete research tasks.

🏢 Customer implementations

Organization Challenge Solution Impact
Arriva UK Trains Critical data was not reaching mobile train and station managers who relied on work mobiles. Sofia Bourika’s team built dynamic, role-based dashboards with mobile-friendly views and scheduled pixel-perfect email reports. Delivered immediate visibility into incidents and operational performance.
Carsa Analytics functioned like a service desk for the used-car retailer. Tobi Daramola’s team constructed a single governed data layer with metrics defined once. Metrics are consumed consistently by both Amazon Quick and AI assistants.

#AmazonQuick #AWS #AgenticAI #DataAnalytics #UserGroup

Source: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026 | Amazon Web Services

item.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026 Shows Tripling of Commits and Pull Requests Driven by Agentic Engineering
item.description:
GitHub Octoverse 2026 Shows Tripling of Commits and Pull Requests Driven by Agentic Engineering

GitHub’s 2026 Octoverse report, announced by EVP Jay Parikh, reveals a sharp rise in development activity that the report links to the rise of “agentic engineering.”

📈 Overview

  • The report describes a “pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub.”
  • Growth is most pronounced in the second half of the year.

📊 Key Metrics

Metric Monthly Value (2026)
Merged pull requests 220 million
Commits 7.38 billion
New repositories 30.3 million

🤖 Agentic Engineering Impact

  • Agentic engineering is cited as the primary driver behind the observed surge in activity.

🛠️ AI‑Powered Methodology

  • Location normalization: LLM classification extracts ISO 3166‑1 alpha‑2 country codes from user profiles to adjust for VPN‑related bias.
  • Industry classification: A fine‑tuned multilingual embedding model maps public repositories (2022‑2026) to NAICS sectors using name, description, topics, and README.
  • Interoperability detection: Repositories are counted when their metadata mentions terms such as “interoperability,” “reverse engineering,” “clean room implementation,” “drop‑in replacement,” or “protocol re‑implementation.”

🌐 Industry & Interoperability Insights

  • The report breaks out activity by industry, based on the NAICS‑sector classification.
  • Separate counts are provided for repositories involving interoperability or reverse engineering.

#GitHub #Octoverse #AgenticEngineering #LLM

item.title: ONE Data Launches Development Finance Observatory AI Platform
item.description:
ONE Data Launches Development Finance Observatory AI Platform

ONE Data, an initiative of the ONE Campaign, launched the Development Finance Observatory on October 14, 2026 during the World Bank‑IMF Annual Meetings. The AI platform is supported by The Rockefeller Foundation and Google.org and aims to give free, rapid access to global aid, lending and debt data.

🔍 Overview

  • The Development Finance Observatory is an AI‑powered data analyst that brings together fragmented development finance data in one place.
  • It is described as “a world‑class data analyst in your pocket.”
  • The platform is built on Google’s Data Commons and supported by the Rockefeller Foundation’s independent charitable affiliate RF Catalytic Capital (RFCC).

🧩 How it works

  • The platform unifies isolated datasets—from the International Monetary Fund, World Bank, Organisation for Economic Co‑operation and Development, and other sources—into a single AI‑ready foundation.
  • Users can query the data with natural‑language questions instead of navigating raw spreadsheets, turning analyses that previously took months into minutes.
  • Every number is traceable to a specific source, preventing AI‑hallucinations.
  • Calculations and visualizations that used to take months now take minutes.

⚙️ Key details

  • Launch date: October 14, 2026, Washington, D.C.
  • Funding: $4 million in combined funding from ONE Data, Google.org and The Rockefeller Foundation (announced in January).
  • Technology partner: Built on Data Commons by Google with support from RFCC.
  • Initiative: Part of ONE Data, which “transforms fragmented, inaccessible development data into trusted, actionable insights for policymakers, campaigners, journalists, and citizens.”

🚀 Availability

  • The platform is publicly available, offering free, rapid access to aid, lending and debt data for governments, journalists, think tanks and the public.
  • Users can ask natural‑language questions and receive answers in seconds with confidence that the answers are correct.

💡 Why it matters

  • The observatory gives leaders a clearer picture of aid, debt, private capital and other financial flows, enabling faster, smarter decisions about where limited resources can have the greatest impact.
  • As the development finance landscape is “being rewritten in real time,” transparent, accountable data is essential for building a more effective system.
  • Quotes from stakeholders:

    “We believe policy makers — who make decisions that impact millions of people’s lives– deserve world class insights.” said David McNair, Managing Director of ONE Data. “We built the Development Finance Observatory so that policymakers, journalists and citizens can get the answers they need in seconds — with the confidence that those answers are right. “Data Commons was built so organizations like ONE can focus on solving the world’s biggest challenges without worrying about data storage and APIs,” Prem Ramaswami, Head of Google Data Commons, said. “The development finance landscape is being rewritten in real time, and we cannot build a better system without understanding how money is actually moving,” said Mike Muldoon, Chief Executive Officer of RFCC, The Rockefeller Foundation’s independent charitable affiliate.

#developmentfinance #AI #dataanalytics #publicpolicy

Source: ONE Data Launches AI Platform That Transforms International Development Sector

item.title: Qlik Deploys Grounded Enterprise AI Assistant on Amazon Bedrock
item.description:
Qlik Deploys Grounded Enterprise AI Assistant on Amazon Bedrock

Qlik has launched Qlik Answers, an AI‑driven assistant built on Amazon Bedrock that lets any employee ask natural‑language questions and receive grounded, sourced answers from multiple data sources.

🔍 Overview

  • Employees face an overload of data, not a shortage of it.
  • Qlik Answers provides a single place to ask questions and get answers drawn from knowledge bases, live analytics apps, glossaries, or documents.
  • The system automatically selects the appropriate source for each query.

🎯 Challenges Addressed

  • Specialized reasoning without latency – orchestrating expert agents while keeping response time low.
  • Varied enterprise queries – handling quick lookups, structured analytics, unstructured documents, glossary definitions, or automations.
  • Avoiding a monolithic assistant – preventing speed and accuracy degradation as capabilities grow.
  • Data‑sovereignty compliance – supporting Europe, APAC, and the Americas with regional builds rather than a single global deployment.
  • Capacity forecasting – predicting token consumption and model availability 3–6 months ahead and validating against real usage.

🏗️ Architecture & Technology

Component Function
Lightweight routing layer Reads the user’s message and context, makes a fast, accurate routing decision (does not solve the task itself).
Shared swarm runtime Defines how specialist agents, tools, state, and human‑in‑the‑loop steps work; enables adding new specialists without reinventing orchestration.
Amazon OpenSearch Service Stores and searches unstructured document content that grounds answers to knowledge‑base and document questions.
Amazon Bedrock (LLM gateway) Provides chat, streaming, embeddings, and reranking capabilities.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails Applies content filtering for prompt injection, PII, secrets, denied topics, and performs grounding‑validation on generated answers.
Amazon SageMaker AI (fallback) Hosts models not yet available in‑Region on Bedrock, then migrates them back once regional availability is released.

🚀 Adoption & Impact

  • General availability began in February 2026; the solution moved from early capability to daily use.
  • Qlik’s Discovery Agent has surfaced more than 100,000 anomalies and outliers for customers since launch.
  • The majority of Qlik Cloud accounts that have agentic tools enabled are actively using them.

📈 Customer Benefits

Customer Deployment Detail Benefit
Bystronic AI chatbot deployed in 15 minutes Employees can query real‑time operations data and receive sourced answers across departments.
Lintech International Indexed more than 17,000 technical documents in Qlik Answers Manual research time cut, response speed up 75 %, managers regain up to 7 hours per week.
TouchPoint Support Services Serves 650 healthcare sites, providing guidance to 15,000 staff Fast, compliance‑aligned guidance in regulated, fast‑paced environments.

📅 Availability & Capacity Planning

  • Qlik forecasts token consumption and model availability 3–6 months before major launches.
  • These forecasts are validated against actual usage once customers start using the product, ensuring adoption growth does not create capacity problems.

#QlikAnswers #AmazonBedrock #EnterpriseAI

Source: How Qlik built grounded, enterprise-scale AI with Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Sage Launches Financial Symphony to Advocate for Explainable AI in Finance
item.description:
Sage Launches Financial Symphony to Advocate for Explainable AI in Finance

Sage has launched Financial Symphony, a classical electro-acoustic composition generated from real, anonymised business data. The project serves as a tangible expression of the company’s “Glass Box” approach to artificial intelligence, highlighting the necessity of explainable AI outputs in the financial and business sectors.

🔍 Overview

The premise of Sage’s campaign is that AI outputs used in business and finance should be inspectable, traceable, and explainable, rather than accepted as the results of an opaque black box. The company aims to make a serious point about AI in finance: an answer is not enough if a finance professional cannot understand how the technology reached it.

⚙️ How it works

The Financial Symphony project translates data into a musical performance using the following elements:

  • Collaboration: Developed alongside data sonification specialist Loud Numbers.
  • Performance: Played by a live string quartet.
  • Data translation: Translates changes in financial metrics into pitch, tempo, and volume.
  • Input: Generated using real, anonymised business data.

💡 Why it matters

Sage’s research highlights a significant trust gap and administrative burden regarding unexplained AI tools in the industry:

  • Decision rejection: Sage’s research found that 71% of finance leaders reject AI-driven decisions they cannot explain.
  • Time spent validating: Finance professionals spend more than 12 hours a week reconstructing logic, validating figures, and defending AI-generated conclusions.

#ExplainableAI #Fintech #Sage #DataSonification

Source: This Week’s Top 5 Stories in Fintech

item.title: Amazon Quick Sight Introduces Hierarchy Filter for Streamlined Dashboards
item.description:
Amazon Quick Sight Introduces Hierarchy Filter for Streamlined Dashboards

Amazon Quick Sight is a fully managed, cloud-native business intelligence (BI) capability for building and publishing interactive dashboards.

Today, we’re announcing the hierarchy filter in Quick Sight.

🔍 Overview

  • “With it, authors can offer rich, multi-level filtering in a single compact control, reducing clutter and guiding readers to the data they need in fewer steps.”
  • “Reduces visual clutter: Instead of showing hundreds of cities upfront, readers see a short list of Regions first.”
  • “Fewer steps and more guided exploration: Readers drill down a logical path (Region → Sub-Region → Country → City) rather than scanning a flat list of dozens of filters.”

🧩 How it works

  • “In the Filters pane, choose Add and select the field to filter on (for example, Region).”
  • “Choose the filter to open Edit filter, open the Filter type menu, and under ADVANCED FILTER choose Hierarchy filter.”
  • “Quick Sight describes it as “Organize and present filter values in a hierarchical tree control.””
  • “A hierarchy filter is a single filter that holds several related fields: up to five levels (for example, Region → Subregion → Country → City → Town).”
  • “The fields don’t need to be geographic. Any parent‑child dimensions work, such as Product Category → Product.”
  • “Under FIELD HIERARCHY, choose Add field to add Region, Country, and City.”
  • “Arrange the fields from broadest to most detailed: Region, then Country, then City. Use each field’s move up and move down control to reorder them. The order sets the reader’s drill‑down path.”

⚙️ Key details

  • “Mix‑and‑match hierarchy selection: Readers can combine levels of the hierarchy in one filter control, selecting an entire country such as Japan alongside a single city such as New York.”
  • “Scales without overwhelming: You can support deep hierarchies (up to five levels) without adding five independent filter controls that crowd the toolbar. One compact control handles the full drill path.”
  • “Prevents reader confusion: Readers don’t need to know which country belongs to which Region. The hierarchy encodes that knowledge for them, making the dashboard self‑guiding.”

Existing filter landscape

Filter Count Types
6 Four geographical filters (Region, Sub‑Region, Country, City) and two more that cover the Segment and Product dimensions

🚀 Getting started

  • “You need author access to create and manage analyses and dashboards.”
  • “For this walkthrough we use a retail sales dataset with a three‑level geographic hierarchy plus a couple of metrics.”
  • “The dataset covers three Regions (EMEA, AMER, APAC), eight countries, and fourteen cities, so the cascade has enough depth to be meaningful.”
  • “We will build a single‑sheet dashboard so the reader can see the whole cascade at a glance.”

💡 Why it matters

  • Reduces visual clutter.
  • Shortens the number of steps to reach target data.
  • Allows flexible, mixed‑level selections.
  • Enables deep hierarchies without crowding the UI.
  • Provides self‑guiding navigation for readers.

#AmazonQuickSight #BI #DataVisualization #Filters

Source: Simplify dashboard drill-down with the Amazon Quick Sight hierarchy filter | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Mastering Prompt Engineering for AI Features in Amazon Quick
item.description:
Mastering Prompt Engineering for AI Features in Amazon Quick

Amazon Quick is providing guidance on prompt engineering to improve the accuracy and reliability of its AI-powered features. This information is being released as a two-part series, with the first part focusing on universal principles and reusable frameworks applicable across all Quick components.

💡 Why it matters

The way prompts are structured directly shapes the quality of output when querying data through conversational analytics, authoring automation flows, or building custom agents. Specificity eliminates assumptions the AI would otherwise make. For example, replacing a vague request to “analyze customer data” with a detailed request defining metrics, timeframes, scope, and decision context transforms generic summaries into actionable intelligence.

🧩 How it works

To produce consistent, high-quality results, the following foundational principles are recommended:

  • Be Specific: Define metrics, timeframes, scope, analysis types, and decision contexts.
  • Provide Business Context: Include information such as who will use the output and what decisions it informs to calibrate the AI’s response.
  • Few-Shot Learning: Show the AI concrete models of the desired output format rather than describing requirements in abstract terms.
  • Shared Vocabulary: Developing a shared prompt vocabulary allows successful framing patterns to become reusable assets across a team.

⚙️ Key details

For sophisticated enterprise interactions, Amazon Quick utilizes structured frameworks to ensure completeness and consistency:

Framework Application Focus Areas
CRISPE Complex requests Comprehensive template across Quick components
RADAR Knowledge retrieval Retrieval strategy, Analysis approach, Document targeting, Answer formation, and Reasoning transparency
ARCHITECT Custom agents Agent identity, Response parameters, Context/knowledge, Special cases, Interaction patterns, Tool/action usage, Ethical guidelines, Improvement, and Validation

These frameworks support various Quick capabilities, including:

  • Amazon Quick Research: Draws from Quick Index, 200+ news outlets, and premium datasets (S&P Global, FactSet, IDC, US Patent data, and PubMed) to deliver structured reports with citations.

item.title: AWS Introduces Serverless Automation for Git Metrics and AI-DLC Observability
item.description:
AWS Introduces Serverless Automation for Git Metrics and AI-DLC Observability

AWS has introduced a serverless approach to automate the collection of Git metrics from GitHub and GitLab. This solution integrates with Amazon Quick Sight to provide live analytics and align with the observability pillar of the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework.

💡 Why it matters

Git activity provides continuous observability into development analytics, but extracting these metrics at scale has traditionally required dedicated infrastructure and hand-rolled extract, transform, and load (ETL) jobs. According to the AI-DLC framework, organizations using AI coding tools need numbers to quantify if AI is increasing speed, merely padding commit counts, or introducing unexpected quality issues.

🧩 How it works

The solution implements an automated, event-driven pipeline using six core AWS services:

Service Function
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Starts the workflow at a configured interval using rate() or cron() expressions.
AWS Step Functions Orchestrates the collection workflow and decides between full and incremental loads.
AWS Lambda Handles separate chunks of repository processing.
AWS Secrets Manager Securely stores Git tokens.
Amazon S3 Persists results for visualization.
Amazon Quick Sight Provides interactive dashboards for graphical visualization.

⚙️ Key details

The architecture includes several specialized mechanisms for efficient data collection:

  • Intelligent change detection: A detector function monitors GitLab activity feeds and the GitHub events API to identify changes in commits, pull requests, issues, or repository creation and deletion.
  • Full and incremental loads: The system performs a full load of all repository metadata on the first execution and triggers a full refresh every 24 hours. Incremental loads collect only data changed since the last run to reduce execution time and API calls.
  • Adaptive chunking: For organizations with more than 20 repositories, the workload is automatically partitioned into parallel chunks processed concurrently via Step Functions Map states.
  • Infrastructure: The serverless design abstracts infrastructure management to remain low-cost at scale.

#AWS #GitMetrics #AIDLC #Serverless #DevOps

Source: A serverless, data-driven Git metrics dashboard using Amazon Quick Sight | Amazon Web Services

item.title: SPICE Up Your Analytics: Master QuickSight Dataset Management in One Dashboard
item.description:
🔍 SPICE Up Your Analytics: Master QuickSight Dataset Management in One Dashboard

𝙎𝙪𝙢𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙮: Struggling with Amazon QuickSight dataset management across multiple regions? This post introduces a comprehensive solution that combines AWS Glue, S3, and Athena to create an automated dashboard that gives you complete visibility into SPICE usage, dataset health, refresh status, and user permissions—all in one place. Say goodbye to manual monitoring and hello to optimized BI performance.

🧭 The QuickSight Management Challenge

Managing Amazon QuickSight across your organization brings a common yet frustrating challenge: how do you efficiently monitor dozens (or hundreds) of datasets spread across multiple regions and accounts?

If you’re like most QuickSight administrators, you’re constantly asking:

  • Is our SPICE refresh running successfully?
  • How much capacity are we consuming?
  • Which dashboards use which datasets?
  • Who has access to what?

The traditional approach—manually clicking through each dataset—quickly becomes unsustainable as your QuickSight environment grows. What if there was a better way?

🔧 Enter the Dataset Insights Solution

The solution we’re exploring automates the collection and visualization of critical QuickSight metadata, giving you a comprehensive dashboard that puts all your dataset insights in one place.

🏗️ How It Works

The architecture consists of three primary components working in harmony:

  1. Data Collection: AWS Glue jobs automatically extract critical information from your QuickSight environment using API calls and CloudWatch metrics.

  2. Data Storage: All extracted metadata is centralized in a dedicated S3 bucket, creating a single source of truth.

  3. Data Visualization: A purpose-built QuickSight dashboard displays actionable insights through Athena-powered queries.

📸 See illustration above showing the comprehensive solution architecture

🧩 What Gets Deployed

When you deploy the solution using the provided CloudFormation templates, you’ll get:

  • Six specialized AWS Glue jobs that extract different aspects of your QuickSight environment
  • A scheduled trigger to automate daily data collection
  • S3 storage for all your QuickSight metadata
  • Pre-configured datasets and data sources in QuickSight
  • A ready-to-use “SPICE Analytics Dashboard” with two information-rich sheets

🌟 Key Benefits and Insights

What makes this solution truly valuable is the comprehensive visibility it provides into your QuickSight environment:

𝗦𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗘 𝗨𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Monitor your SPICE capacity utilization with precision. The dashboard displays current consumption levels and allows you to set up alerts when you approach capacity limits—no more surprises when datasets fail to refresh!

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘀 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴

See at a glance which datasets are refreshing successfully and which have failed. No more hunting through individual dataset logs to find problems.

𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀

Understand the dependencies between your datasets, dashboards, and analyses. This is invaluable when planning changes or troubleshooting issues.

𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁

Get full visibility into who can access what, making security reviews much simpler.

🚀 Getting Started in Four Simple Steps

Implementing this solution is straightforward with the provided CloudFormation templates:

1️⃣ Deploy the Data Collection Infrastructure

Use the first CloudFormation template to create the AWS Glue jobs, IAM roles, and S3 bucket needed for data collection.

1

Launch Stack: spice-usage-glue-jobs-stack

2️⃣ Run the AWS Glue ETL Jobs

After deployment, manually run each AWS Glue job once to collect initial data.

3️⃣ Configure S3 Permissions in QuickSight

Make sure QuickSight has appropriate access to the S3 bucket and Athena.

4️⃣ Deploy QuickSight Assets

Use the second CloudFormation template to create the dashboard, datasets, and data sources in QuickSight.

1

Launch Stack: spice-usage-QS-assets-stack

📸 See screenshot above showing the CloudFormation parameter input screen

Within 12 hours, your dashboard will populate with comprehensive data about your QuickSight environment, giving you unprecedented visibility.

🔮 What This Means for Your BI Strategy

This solution transforms how you manage QuickSight across your organization. Instead of reactive troubleshooting and manual checks, you gain:

  • Proactive monitoring with configurable alerts before issues impact users
  • Data-driven capacity planning based on actual usage patterns
  • Enhanced security oversight through comprehensive access visibility
  • Operational efficiency by quickly identifying orphaned or duplicate resources

The most powerful aspect? Everything is automated. Once set up, the solution will continue to provide fresh insights daily with minimal maintenance required.

🤔 Final Thoughts

As organizations increasingly rely on business intelligence for critical decisions, the infrastructure supporting those insights becomes just as important as the insights themselves. This QuickSight monitoring solution addresses a significant gap in the BI administration workflow.

Whether you’re managing a handful of datasets or hundreds across multiple regions, having a single-pane-of-glass view into your QuickSight environment allows you to focus less on administration and more on driving business value through data.

How much time could your team save with automated QuickSight monitoring?
